title: Production Outage Lessons
description: Study real production outages from major tech companies and learn the patterns that cause cascading failures, plus strategies for building resilient systems.

data.text: Production outages are inevitable in large-scale systems. The difference between resilient and fragile systems is not whether outages happen, but how quickly they are detected, contained, and recovered. Studying real outages teaches you what can go wrong and how to design for failure.

Major outages follow a handful of recurring patterns. Deploying bad code to production is the most common cause. Misconfigured infrastructure, such as wrong capacity limits or missing failover, is a close second. Data corruption and cascading failures complete the top four.

data.title: The Four Horsemen of Outages
items: Deploy failures: Bad code, untested edge cases, or configuration errors reach production
Infrastructure misconfiguration: Capacity limits, security groups, or DNS records set incorrectly
Data corruption: Schema changes, bad migrations, or partial writes corrupt state
Cascading failures: One component fails and overwhelms dependent services

data.title: Cascading Failures
data.text: A cascading failure starts when one service degrades and its clients retry aggressively, overwhelming the struggling service further. Retry storms amplify failures and must be controlled with exponential backoff and circuit breakers.

Each outage reveals design gaps. AWS's retry storm showed the need for load shedding. Cloudflare's router misconfiguration showed the need for staged rollouts. GitHub's data corruption showed the need for backup validation. Facebook's BGP issue showed the need for multi-homing.

data.title: Patterns to Prevent Cascading Failures
items: **Circuit breakers**: Stop calling a failing service after N failures
**Bulkheads**: Isolate critical services so one failure does not consume all resources
**Rate limiting**: Protect services from traffic spikes
**Graceful degradation**: Disable non-essential features under load
**Chaos testing**: Inject failures in staging to find weaknesses before production

terms.definition: A pattern that stops calling a failing service after repeated failures, giving it time to recover.
Isolating resources for different services so one failure does not exhaust shared pools.
Rejecting requests during overload to protect the healthy parts of the system.

data.title: Outage Lessons
points: Outages reveal the gaps between design assumptions and reality
Cascading failures are caused by uncontrolled retries and shared resource exhaustion
Monitoring, alerting, and runbooks reduce detection and response time
Postmortems turn outages into learning opportunities
Chaos engineering finds failure modes before customers do
data.takeaway: Resilient systems are not built by preventing all failures — they are built by expecting failure and designing for rapid recovery.

data.title: Design a Resilient Payment Service
data.description: Design a payment service that must remain available even if the payment gateway fails. Specify the circuit breaker thresholds, fallback behavior, and recovery strategy.
data.expectedOutcome: Circuit breaker opens after 5 consecutive failures. Fallback queues payments for retry. Recovery uses half-open probing to test gateway health before resuming traffic.

items.question: How do you detect an outage before users report it?
items.answer: Use synthetic monitoring that simulates user journeys and alerts on degradation. Combine with real-time dashboards showing error rates, latency percentiles, and system health.

items.question: What is the most important resilience pattern?
items.answer: Circuit breakers are the most critical pattern. Without them, retry storms turn slow failures into total outages. Always implement circuit breakers on external dependencies.
